title: Protagoras
orientation: This chapter covers Protagoras and the Sophists, the sceptical movement that confronted the great pre-Socratic systems in the later fifth century B.C. Russell situates the Sophists socially and politically as paid teachers of practical, especially forensic (law-court), skills to the Athenian rich, examines Protagoras's famous relativist doctrine that 'man is the measure of all things,' and defends the Sophists against what he presents as unfair and largely Plato-driven vilification, while also tracing the darker political and military history of late fifth-century Athens that forms their backdrop.
historical_background: Russell places the Sophists' rise against the backdrop of Athenian democracy's political triumph without any corresponding redistribution of aristocratic wealth, so that the rich, who had education, leisure, and travel, embodied Hellenic culture while poorer citizens viewed them with a mixture of envy and traditionalist suspicion. In Athenian law-courts, ordinary citizens served as judges chosen by lot, and litigants argued their own cases, creating high demand for training in oratory and argument, which the Sophists supplied for a fee. Protagoras, born about 500 B.C. at Abdera (Democritus's home city), twice visited Athens (the second visit no later than 432 B.C.), made a law-code for Thurii in 444-3 B.C., and, despite writing an agnostic book On the Gods, was probably never actually prosecuted for impiety, unlike Anaxagoras. The chapter closes with a fuller historical survey: the Persian Wars, Periclean prosperity and the deaths of Pericles and his circle in the plague, the Peloponnesian War (431-404 B.C.), Athenian atrocities such as the destruction of Melos (416 B.C.), the naval defeat at Aegospotami (405 B.C.), the oligarchic Thirty Tyrants (some, including Critias, former pupils of Socrates), the restoration of democracy, and finally the trial and execution of Socrates (399 B.C.).
philosophical_problems: Is there objective truth that exists independently of what individuals or societies believe, or is 'man the measure of all things'?
Can moral and legal relativism be reconciled with a practical defense of law, convention, and traditional morality?
Should the pursuit of truth follow an argument wherever it leads, even against edifying or socially comfortable conclusions?
Is justice merely 'the interest of the stronger,' or is there an impersonal standard beyond power?
What is the relationship between intellectual/cultural innovation and political conservatism or radicalism?

philosophers_discussed.name: Protagoras
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Chief of the Sophists and the chapter's central figure; famous for the doctrine that 'man is the measure of all things,' interpreted as denying objective truth where men differ; despite his theoretical scepticism about the gods, he defended law, convention, and traditional morality and worship on practical grounds.

philosophers_discussed.name: Plato
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Presented by Russell as the chief source, and chief critic, of the Sophists, caricaturing and vilifying them (e.g. in the Euthydemus, the Sophist, the Protagoras, the Theaetetus, the Republic, the Gorgias); Russell accuses Plato of intellectual dishonesty, twisting arguments toward conclusions he judges virtuous rather than following them wherever they lead.

philosophers_discussed.name: Gorgias
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A Sophist noted for the extreme sceptical thesis that nothing exists, that if anything exists it is unknowable, and that even if knowable it could not be communicated to others.

philosophers_discussed.name: Thrasymachus
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A figure in Plato's Republic (Book I) who argues that justice is nothing but the interest of the stronger, that laws serve the advantage of governments, and that there is no impersonal standard of justice.

philosophers_discussed.name: Callicles
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A figure in Plato's Gorgias who similarly holds that the law of nature is the law of the stronger, with conventional institutions and morality invented merely to restrain the strong for the convenience of the weak.

philosophers_discussed.name: F.C.S. Schiller
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A modern (early twentieth-century) founder of pragmatism who called himself a disciple of Protagoras, drawing on the Theaetetus's suggestion that one opinion can be 'better' than another even if not 'truer.'

philosophers_discussed.name: Socrates
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Appears at the chapter's edges: as a defendant in Plato's dialogues that dramatize encounters with the Sophists, as one of the very few Athenian-born philosophers/mathematicians of the century, and as the eventual victim (399 B.C.) of the same climate of political prosecution that earlier struck Anaxagoras.

core_concepts.name: The Sophists as a social and professional class
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The word 'Sophist' originally just meant something like our word 'professor': a paid teacher who taught wealthy young men practical skills, especially the skills needed to win in law courts and assemblies.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A class of professional itinerant teachers in fifth-century Greece who, in the absence of public education, taught for a fee the sons of those with private means, chiefly the arts of argument and oratory useful in the law-courts and political life, without founding schools, brotherhoods, or esoteric doctrines as other philosophical traditions did.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: The Sophists' social position (paid teachers of the rich, unattached to religious or communal traditions) explains both their popularity with one class and their deep unpopularity, later amplified by Plato, with another, and it marks a new, secular model of intellectual life distinct from the quasi-religious philosophical schools that preceded them.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Arose from the practical demands of Athenian legal and political life, in which litigants argued their own cases before large panels of ordinary citizen-judges chosen by lot.
examples: Athenian litigants hiring Sophists to write speeches or teach forensic skill
Protagoras's alleged fee arrangement tied to his student's first legal victory
objections: Plato devoted himself, in Russell's view unfairly, to caricaturing and vilifying the Sophists.
The general public viewed them with hostility rooted partly in class resentment and traditionalism.
competing_positions: The older model of a philosophical school as a quasi-religious brotherhood with common life and esoteric doctrine, which the Sophists explicitly lacked
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell compares the Sophists' social role to that of modern corporation lawyers, who similarly serve the interests of a wealthy class through specialized argumentative skill.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Tied to Athenian democracy's legal system and to class conflict between the cultured rich and the traditionalist, envious poor.

core_concepts.name: 'Man is the measure of all things' (Protagorean relativism)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Protagoras's most famous claim is that truth is relative to each individual: things are, for you, as they appear to you, and things are, for me, as they appear to me, with no independent fact that could show one of us wrong.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Protagoras's doctrine, 'Man is the measure of all things, of things that are that they are, and of things that are not that they are not,' interpreted by Russell as meaning each individual man is the measure of all things, so that when men differ in their judgments there is no objective truth by which one can be shown right and the other wrong; the doctrine is essentially sceptical and rests on the 'deceitfulness' of the senses.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is the founding statement of philosophical relativism in the Western tradition and, via the Theaetetus's jaundice example, an ancestor of pragmatist ideas about the practical grounds for preferring one belief over another even without a fact of the matter about which is 'truer.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: Formulated by Protagoras and discussed by Plato in the Theaetetus.
examples: Plato's jaundice example: everything looks yellow to a man with jaundice; we cannot say things are really not yellow, only that the healthy man's perception is 'better' because health is better than sickness
competing_positions: Objective theories of truth assumed by most earlier pre-Socratic philosophers, who sought a single correct metaphysical account of reality
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: F.C.S. Schiller, one of the founders of modern pragmatism, called himself a disciple of Protagoras on the basis of this doctrine's pragmatist-friendly reading in the Theaetetus.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Led Protagoras, despite his professed uncertainty about the gods, to defend traditional worship and morality on the practical ground that the majority's beliefs and conventions should be followed.

core_concepts.name: Protagoras's practical defense of convention despite scepticism
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Even though Protagoras said he could not be sure whether the gods exist, he still thought people ought to worship them, and he generally supported following established laws and customs.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Protagoras's position that, since there is no objective truth to appeal to, the majority becomes for practical purposes the arbiter of belief, which led him to defend law, convention, and traditional morality, including worship of gods whose existence he professed himself unable to affirm or deny.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell presents this as 'the right' position for a thoroughgoing and logical theoretical sceptic to hold, since without an objective standard, practical and social convention is the only available guide to action.
examples: Protagoras's opening line from On the Gods: 'With regard to the gods, I cannot feel sure either that they are or that they are not...'
competing_positions: Thrasymachus's and Callicles's more radical position, that justice/law is merely the interest of the stronger, which Russell explicitly says is not characteristic of the Sophists generally
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly reconciles theoretical scepticism about the gods with practical religious and social conservatism.

core_concepts.name: Sceptical extremes among the Sophists: Gorgias's nihilism
core_concepts.plain_explanation: One Sophist, Gorgias, pushed scepticism to an extreme: he argued nothing exists, that even if something did exist we could not know it, and that even if we could know it we could never explain it to anyone else.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Gorgias's three-part sceptical/nihilist thesis: (1) nothing exists; (2) if anything exists, it is unknowable; (3) even granting that one man could know it, he could never communicate it to others.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Illustrates, for Russell, the genuine intellectual rigor and willingness to follow argument to uncomfortable conclusions that he thinks characterized the best Sophists, in contrast to their popular reputation for mere cleverness or immorality.
competing_positions: Protagoras's more moderate relativism, which still preserves practical grounds for belief and action

core_concepts.name: 'Might makes right' doctrines (Thrasymachus and Callicles)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Two figures in Plato's dialogues argue that justice is really nothing but whatever benefits the powerful, and that laws restraining the strong are just a convenient trick invented by the weak.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Thrasymachus's position (Republic, Book I) that there is no justice except the interest of the stronger and that laws are made by governments for their own advantage, with no impersonal standard for appeal; and Callicles's similar position (Gorgias) that the law of nature is the law of the stronger, with conventional institutions and moral precepts invented by the weak to restrain the strong.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell explicitly notes these doctrines have won wider assent in the twentieth century (his own day) than in antiquity, and stresses that, whatever their merit, they are 'not characteristic of the Sophists' as a whole, correcting a common conflation.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Attributed by Plato to Thrasymachus and Callicles as dramatic interlocutors.
competing_positions: Protagoras's practical defense of law and convention as socially necessary, which is not a might-makes-right position
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes, writing in the 1940s, that such doctrines 'have won much wider assent in our day than they did in antiquity,' a clear contemporary allusion.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly concerns the foundations of political legitimacy and law.

arguments.title: Protagoras's relativist argument from 'man is the measure'
premises: The senses are deceitful and give different, sometimes conflicting, appearances to different perceivers.
There is no standard beyond individual appearance/judgment by which one perceiver's view could be shown objectively truer than another's.
'Man is the measure of all things, of things that are that they are, and of things that are not that they are not.'
arguments.conclusion: When men differ in their judgments, there is no objective truth in virtue of which one is right and the other wrong; each man's perception/judgment is true for him.
arguments.explanation: Russell reads this doctrine as essentially sceptical, resting on distrust of the senses' reliability. He notes an important refinement suggested by Plato in the Theaetetus: even if one opinion cannot be objectively 'truer' than another, it can still be 'better,' as when a healthy man's undistorted perception is preferable to a jaundiced man's, because health is better than sickness. This refinement is what connects Protagoras to modern pragmatism via F.C.S. Schiller.
implications: Undermines any claim to a single correct metaphysical or scientific account of reality, in contrast to the confident cosmological claims of the earlier pre-Socratics.
Pushes ethics and politics toward convention and majority practice as the only available practical standard, since no objective standard is available.

arguments.title: Thrasymachus's 'justice is the interest of the stronger' argument
premises: Laws in any state are made by whoever holds governing power.
Those in power make laws to serve their own advantage.
'Justice' is defined, in practice, as obedience to the laws.
arguments.conclusion: There is no justice beyond the interest of the stronger (the ruling power), and no impersonal standard to which weaker parties can appeal in contests for power.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as a distinct and more radical position than Protagoras's, arising from the same general climate of sceptical questioning that the Sophists encouraged, though he is careful to say it is not typical of the Sophists as a class.
implications: Anticipates later political realist or power-based theories of law and justice, which Russell notes had, by his own time, gained much wider acceptance than in antiquity.

key_distinctions: Objective truth versus relative, individually- or socially-grounded belief
An opinion being 'truer' versus an opinion being 'better' (the pragmatist reading of Protagoras via the jaundice example)
Protagoras's moderate, convention-preserving relativism versus Thrasymachus's and Callicles's radical 'might makes right' positions
The Sophists as paid, unaffiliated teachers of argument versus older philosophical schools organized as quasi-religious brotherhoods with esoteric doctrine
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: The Sophists, with Protagoras as chief, confront 'the great pre-Socratic systems' surveyed in earlier chapters with a sceptical movement; Protagoras came from Abdera, the same city as Democritus, and part of Democritus's philosophy (covered in the preceding chapter) was explicitly intended as an answer to Protagoras.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Plato's extensive, largely hostile engagement with the Sophists (in the Euthydemus, Sophist, Protagoras, Theaetetus, Republic, and Gorgias) shapes nearly all surviving evidence about them; Russell argues this hostility introduced a lasting 'vice' into philosophy, of judging doctrines by their social or ethical consequences rather than following argument wherever it leads. In the twentieth century, F.C.S. Schiller explicitly revived Protagoras as a forerunner of pragmatism, and Russell notes that 'might makes right' doctrines associated with Thrasymachus and Callicles have found much wider acceptance in modern times than in antiquity.
political_social_context: Athenian democracy was politically triumphant but left aristocratic wealth untouched, producing class tension between a cultured, often impious rich and a poorer citizenry given to both envy and cultural traditionalism; Russell draws an extended analogy to early twentieth-century America, likening the Sophists' defense of the wealthy's interests to the modern role of corporation lawyers, and Tammany-style traditionalist politics to Athenian popular conservatism. The chapter also surveys the political and military history of late fifth-century Athens: the Persian Wars, the Periclean building program, the plague and deaths of Pericles and his sons, the Peloponnesian War (431-404 B.C.), the destruction of Melos (416 B.C.), the failed Sicilian expedition (from 414 B.C.), the naval defeat at Aegospotami (405 B.C.), the oligarchic rule of the Thirty Tyrants (some former pupils of Socrates), the restoration of democracy under an amnesty, and Socrates's trial and execution (399 B.C.).
religion_science_culture_context: Protagoras's lost book On the Gods opened with agnostic uncertainty about the gods' existence and nature, yet he defended traditional worship in practice. Euripides is noted as influenced by Protagoras and the free-thinking spirit of the age, his Trojan Women read as a protest against Athenian wartime atrocity (the destruction of Melos); Aristophanes satirized Socrates, the Sophists, and philosophers generally while remaining on friendly personal terms with them, per Plato's Symposium.
russell_presentation: Russell presents Protagoras as chief of a sceptical movement, the Sophists, that confronted the confident metaphysical systems of the earlier pre-Socratics in the later fifth century B.C. He situates the Sophists socially as paid professional teachers of the rich, supplying oratorical and argumentative skills needed in Athenian law-courts and politics, and explains the class-based hostility they attracted, comparing their social role to that of modern corporation lawyers. Turning to Protagoras's doctrines, Russell explains 'man is the measure of all things' as a thoroughgoing relativism grounded in distrust of the senses, denying objective truth wherever men differ, while noting Plato's Theaetetus suggests a pragmatist-friendly refinement (one opinion can be 'better,' if not 'truer,' than another), which the modern pragmatist F.C.S. Schiller drew on directly. Russell stresses that Protagoras's theoretical scepticism about objective truth and about the gods coexisted with a practical defense of law, convention, and traditional worship, a combination Russell calls the logically correct stance for a consistent sceptic. He defends the Sophists generally against what he considers Plato's unfair and often intellectually dishonest vilification, arguing Plato allowed himself to judge doctrines by their edifying social consequences rather than following arguments wherever they led, a vice Russell says entered philosophy through Plato and persisted afterward. Russell distinguishes Protagoras's moderate position from more radical Sophistic or Sophist-adjacent doctrines, Gorgias's extreme scepticism, and Thrasymachus's and Callicles's 'might makes right' theories of justice, explicitly noting the latter are not typical of the Sophists as a class, though they have found much wider modern acceptance than they did in antiquity. The chapter closes with an extended historical narrative of Athens from the Persian Wars through Pericles's death, the Peloponnesian War, wartime atrocities (Melos), military defeat (Aegospotami), the oligarchic Thirty Tyrants, the restoration of democracy, and finally the trial and execution of Socrates in 399 B.C., which Russell presents as the culmination of the embittered political climate this chapter describes.
critical_context: Russell explicitly labels his own extended parallel between fifth-century Athens and early twentieth-century America (Sophists/corporation lawyers, democratic traditionalists/Tammany) as an interpretive analogy of his own devising, not part of the ancient source material; he further concedes it is imperfect, noting 'the enlightened are politically weaker in America than they were in Athens, because they have failed to make common cause with the plutocracy.' Readers should treat this comparison as Russell's own early-1940s political commentary rather than as historical fact about antiquity.
key_takeaways: The Sophists, led by Protagoras, were paid professional teachers who taught the Athenian rich practical skills, especially oratory and argument useful in law-courts and politics, in a period of Athenian democracy that left aristocratic wealth intact.
Protagoras's central doctrine, 'man is the measure of all things,' is a form of relativism denying objective truth where individuals' judgments differ, grounded in distrust of the senses.

Despite his theoretical uncertainty about the gods and about objective truth, Protagoras defended traditional worship, law, and convention on practical grounds, which Russell calls the logically consistent position for a thoroughgoing sceptic.

Russell defends the Sophists against Plato's largely hostile portrayal, arguing Plato judged doctrines by their social consequences rather than following arguments to their conclusions, introducing a lasting intellectual vice into philosophy.

More radical doctrines like Gorgias's total scepticism and Thrasymachus's and Callicles's 'might makes right' theories of justice are distinguished from, and are not typical of, the Sophists generally.

The chapter's historical survey (Peloponnesian War, the massacre at Melos, defeat at Aegospotami, the Thirty Tyrants, and Socrates's trial and death in 399 B.C.) shows the darkening political backdrop against which Sophistic scepticism and, later, Socratic and Platonic philosophy developed.
study_notes:
This chapter marks a genuine turning point in Russell's narrative: the confident, cosmology-building pre-Socratic systems (Ionians, Pythagoreans, Parmenides, Empedocles, Anaxagoras, the Atomists) give way to a sceptical movement that questions whether such confident metaphysical claims are even possible. Protagoras's 'man is the measure' doctrine should be understood as a direct response to the proliferation of rival, incompatible cosmological systems surveyed in the preceding chapters: if Heraclitus, Parmenides, Empedocles, Anaxagoras, and the Atomists cannot agree on the nature of reality, perhaps (Protagoras suggests) there simply is no single objective truth about it, only differing human perspectives.

A second important thread is Russell's sociological account of the Sophists. Unlike earlier philosophical traditions descended from Orphism, which organized themselves as quasi-religious brotherhoods with esoteric doctrines, the Sophists were freelance professionals who taught argument itself, for a fee, without committing to any particular conclusion. This is central to understanding why they were unpopular in two very different ways: with ordinary citizens, who resented their association with the rich and their perceived impiety; and with Plato, who (per Russell) objected on more intellectual grounds to their willingness to argue any side of a question rather than pursue what Plato considered virtuous conclusions.

When studying Protagoras's relativism, keep two distinct claims separate: (1) the strict relativist claim that no opinion is objectively truer than another; and (2) the softer, pragmatist-friendly claim (drawn from the Theaetetus's jaundice example) that one opinion can still be practically better than another. It is claim (2) that Russell says inspired the modern pragmatist F.C.S. Schiller to call himself a disciple of Protagoras, and it is worth being able to explain why claim (2) does not simply collapse back into claim (1).

Finally, note how the chapter's second half shifts from doctrine to narrative history. Russell uses this history, ending in Socrates's execution, to set up the Socratic and Platonic chapters that follow: the same political climate of prosecution, factional bitterness, and popular suspicion of intellectuals that struck Anaxagoras (previous chapters) and colored the reception of the Sophists ultimately claims Socrates himself.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A paid, traveling teacher in ancient Greece who taught practical skills, especially persuasive speaking and argument, to young men who could afford it.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Originally a neutral term roughly equivalent to 'professor,' denoting a professional teacher, typically without a fixed school or esoteric doctrine, who taught for a fee skills (chiefly rhetoric and argument) useful in law-courts and political life; the term later acquired a negative connotation largely through Plato's polemics.
related_concepts: The Sophists as a social and professional class

glossary_terms.term: Man is the measure of all things
glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Protagoras's famous saying meaning that truth depends on each individual person's own perception or judgment, with no independent standard to say who is right.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Protagoras's relativist thesis, interpreted by Russell as holding that when individuals' judgments conflict, there is no objective truth by which one can be shown correct and the other incorrect, grounded in scepticism about the reliability of sense-perception.
related_concepts: 'Man is the measure of all things' (Protagorean relativism)

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The view that truth or morality is not fixed and universal but depends on the perspective of the individual or culture holding it.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The philosophical position, exemplified by Protagoras, that truth-claims (or moral claims) lack an objective, perspective-independent grounding and are instead relative to the perceiver or the community.
related_concepts: 'Man is the measure of all things' (Protagorean relativism)

glossary_terms.term: 'Might makes right' (justice as the interest of the stronger)
glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that there is no real justice beyond what benefits whoever is powerful enough to enforce their will.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine, attributed by Plato to Thrasymachus and, in different terms, to Callicles, that justice is nothing but the advantage of the ruling power and that law and conventional morality are merely devices, invented either by rulers for their own benefit or by the weak to restrain the strong.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A modern philosophical movement that judges beliefs partly by their practical usefulness or consequences rather than by correspondence to an abstract, fixed truth alone.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A twentieth-century philosophical school, represented here by F.C.S. Schiller, that Russell connects to Protagoras via the Theaetetus's suggestion that opinions can be evaluated as 'better' or 'worse' by their practical fitness even where they cannot be shown objectively 'truer.'
related_concepts: 'Man is the measure of all things' (Protagorean relativism)

questions.prompt: What did the word 'Sophist' originally mean, before it acquired a negative connotation, and what did Sophists actually teach?
questions.answer: It originally meant something like our word 'professor'; Sophists were paid teachers who taught young men, mainly those with private means, skills thought useful in practical life, especially the art of argument and oratory useful in law-courts and politics.
questions.explanation: Russell begins the chapter by correcting the modern pejorative sense of 'Sophist' with this original, neutral meaning.

questions.prompt: State Protagoras's doctrine 'man is the measure of all things' and explain how Russell interprets it.
questions.answer: 'Man is the measure of all things, of things that are that they are, and of things that are not that they are not.' Russell interprets this as meaning each individual man is the measure of all things, so that when men's judgments differ there is no objective truth in virtue of which one is right and the other wrong; the doctrine is essentially sceptical, based on the deceitfulness of the senses.
questions.explanation: This is Protagoras's single most famous doctrine and the chapter's philosophical center.

questions.prompt: Compare the claim that one opinion can be 'truer' than another with the claim (drawn from Plato's Theaetetus) that one opinion can be 'better' than another, using the jaundice example.
questions.answer: Strict relativism denies that any opinion is objectively truer than another. The Theaetetus's softer reading allows that, although we cannot say a jaundiced man's view that everything is yellow is objectively false and the healthy man's view objectively true, we can still say the healthy man's opinion is better, because health is better than sickness; this preserves a practical basis for preferring one view without claiming objective truth.
questions.explanation: This distinction is what links Protagoras to modern pragmatism via F.C.S. Schiller.

questions.prompt: Which Sophist argued that nothing exists, that if anything exists it is unknowable, and that even if knowable it could not be communicated?
questions.explanation: Russell cites Gorgias as an example of a Sophist pushing scepticism to its most extreme, logically rigorous conclusion.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, how did Protagoras reconcile his theoretical scepticism about the gods with his practical stance on religion?
questions.answer: He wrote that he could not be sure whether the gods exist, yet he maintained they ought to be worshipped; Russell calls this the logically consistent position for a thoroughgoing sceptic, since without objective truth, the majority becomes the practical arbiter of what to believe and do.
questions.explanation: This shows Protagoras's characteristic combination of theoretical doubt and practical conservatism.

questions.prompt: Distinguish Protagoras's position from Thrasymachus's and Callicles's 'might makes right' doctrines, and note Russell's own comment on their historical reception.
questions.answer: Protagoras defended law, convention, and traditional morality as practically necessary given the absence of objective truth. Thrasymachus and Callicles instead argued justice is simply the interest of the stronger and that law/morality exist only to restrain the strong for others' convenience. Russell explicitly says such 'might makes right' doctrines are not characteristic of the Sophists as a class, and notes they have won much wider assent in modern times than in antiquity.
questions.explanation: Russell is careful to prevent readers from conflating Protagoras's moderate relativism with these more radical political doctrines.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's criticism of Plato's treatment of the Sophists.
questions.answer: Premise: Plato consistently caricatures and vilifies the Sophists in his dialogues. Premise: Plato is 'hardly ever intellectually honest,' because he judges doctrines by their social/ethical consequences rather than following the argument purely on theoretical grounds, while pretending to do the latter. Conclusion: Plato introduced into philosophy a lasting vice of assuming the conclusions ethical inquiry should reach in advance, a vice that persisted after him.
questions.explanation: This tests whether students can reconstruct Russell's own critical argument about Plato's fairness (or lack of it) toward the Sophists.

questions.prompt: What historical event in 399 B.C. does Russell present as the culmination of the political climate described in this chapter?
questions.answer: The trial and execution of Socrates, occurring in an embittered post-war democracy restored after the fall of the Thirty Tyrants, under an amnesty that barred direct vengeance but left Socrates vulnerable to prosecution on other pretexts.
questions.explanation: Russell ends the chapter's historical survey with this event, linking it to the earlier persecution of Anaxagoras and to the broader climate of suspicion toward intellectuals.

flashcards.back: That Plato was 'hardly ever intellectually honest,' judging doctrines by their social consequences rather than following arguments purely on theoretical grounds, while pretending otherwise.

flashcards.front: What happened to Athens at Melos in 416 B.C.?
flashcards.back: The Athenians conquered the island, killed all men of military age, and enslaved the rest; Euripides's Trojan Women protests this act.

flashcards.front: What was the Thirty Tyrants, and who was among them?
flashcards.back: An oligarchic government the Spartans established in Athens after the Peloponnesian War; Critias, its chief, and some others had been pupils of Socrates.

flashcards.front: In what year, and under what circumstances, was Socrates tried and executed?
flashcards.back: 399 B.C., under a restored but embittered democracy, following the amnesty after the Thirty Tyrants' overthrow.

quiz.prompt: What did the term 'Sophist' originally mean, before acquiring a negative sense?
quiz.explanation: Russell explains that 'Sophist' originally had no bad connotation and meant something close to 'professor,' a paid teacher.
quiz.related_concept: The Sophists as a social and professional class

quiz.prompt: What is the chief doctrine associated with Protagoras discussed in this chapter?
options: The world is made of atoms and void
Man is the measure of all things
Mind is the cause of all motion
quiz.explanation: This relativist formula is Protagoras's most famous and historically important doctrine.
quiz.related_concept: 'Man is the measure of all things' (Protagorean relativism)

quiz.prompt: How does Russell say Protagoras reconciled scepticism about objective truth with support for traditional religion and morality?
options: He rejected all convention as false
He held that, absent objective truth, the majority becomes the practical arbiter of belief, so law and worship should be maintained
He claimed the gods personally revealed truth to him
He argued science should replace religion entirely
quiz.explanation: Protagoras defended convention and traditional worship precisely because his relativism left no objective standard beyond practical, majority-sanctioned belief.
quiz.related_concept: Protagoras's practical defense of convention despite scepticism

quiz.prompt: Russell presents Thrasymachus's and Callicles's 'might makes right' doctrines as typical and representative of the Sophists as a whole.
quiz.explanation: False: Russell explicitly states these doctrines 'are not characteristic of the Sophists,' distinguishing them from Protagoras's more moderate position.

quiz.prompt: Which modern philosophical movement does Russell connect to Protagoras via the Theaetetus's jaundice example?
quiz.explanation: Russell notes F.C.S. Schiller, a founder of pragmatism, called himself a disciple of Protagoras based on the idea that one opinion can be 'better' though not 'truer' than another.
quiz.related_concept: 'Man is the measure of all things' (Protagorean relativism)

quiz.prompt: The Sophist ______ argued that nothing exists, that if anything exists it cannot be known, and that even if it could be known it could never be communicated to others.
quiz.explanation: Gorgias is credited by Russell with this extreme sceptical position.
quiz.related_concept: Sceptical extremes among the Sophists: Gorgias's nihilism

quiz.prompt: According to Russell's criticism, what does Plato allow himself to do when discussing the Sophists' doctrines?
options: Follow arguments purely on theoretical grounds without bias
Judge doctrines by their social/ethical consequences while pretending to follow pure argument
Refuse to engage with Sophist ideas at all
quiz.explanation: Russell accuses Plato of judging doctrines by whether they lead to virtuous conclusions while pretending to be intellectually neutral.
quiz.related_concept: The Sophists as a social and professional class

quiz.prompt: What event does the chapter identify as occurring in 399 B.C., closing its historical survey of late fifth-century Athens?
options: The trial and execution of Socrates
The founding of the Delian League
quiz.explanation: The chapter's historical narrative culminates in Socrates's trial and death in 399 B.C., under the restored but embittered Athenian democracy.

essay_prompts.prompt: Analyze Protagoras's doctrine 'man is the measure of all things.' How does Russell distinguish the strict relativist reading from the pragmatist-friendly reading suggested by the jaundice example in the Theaetetus, and what are the philosophical stakes of that distinction?
rubric: Accurate statement of the Protagorean formula and Russell's interpretation
Accurate explanation of the jaundice example and the 'better vs. truer' distinction
Discussion of the connection to modern pragmatism (F.C.S. Schiller)
Original assessment of whether the distinction successfully rescues Protagoras's doctrine from full relativism

essay_prompts.prompt: Evaluate Russell's defense of the Sophists against Plato's portrayal of them. Does Russell succeed in showing that Plato's hostility was driven by intellectual dishonesty rather than legitimate philosophical or ethical concerns?
rubric: Accurate summary of Plato's main criticisms of the Sophists as reported by Russell
Consideration of possible defenses of Plato

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare Protagoras's practical defense of law and convention with Thrasymachus's and Callicles's 'might makes right' theories of justice. Are these positions compatible extensions of Sophistic scepticism, or fundamentally different responses to it?
rubric: Accurate account of Protagoras's position and its grounding in his relativism
Accurate account of Thrasymachus's and Callicles's positions
Clear comparison highlighting similarities and differences
Reference to Russell's explicit statement that the latter are not typical of the Sophists
